450.quote_or_event: “You might just as well take the sun out of the sky as friendship from life; for the immortal gods have given us nothing better or more delightful.”
450.explanation: Laelius answers philosophers who advise holding friendship loosely to avoid anxiety, or seeking it only for advantage: to remove friendship from life, he says, is like removing the sun from the sky.
450.tie_back: Like the Kural, Cicero treats the loss of good friends as a darkness that no other good can make up for, though he does not weigh it against the enmity of many.
450.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia (On Friendship), §47 (ch. 13) (tr. E. S. Shuckburgh)
450._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Shuckburgh translation on Project Gutenberg (eBook #2808). Strong agreement on the supreme value of friendship and the ruin of losing it; the Kural's specific 'ten times worse than the enmity of many' comparison has no counterpart in Cicero.

463.quote_or_event: “It is, therefore, only a madman who, in a calm, would pray for a storm; a wise man's way is, when the storm does come, to withstand it with all the means at his command, and especially, when the advantages to be expected in case of a successful issue are greater than the hazards of the struggle.”
463.explanation: Cicero warns against exposing oneself to danger needlessly and says a risk is worth running only when the gain to be expected from success outweighs what is hazarded.
463.tie_back: Shares the Kural's rule that the wise weigh what may be lost against what may be gained, and do not court ruin for the sake of a hoped-for profit.
463.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §83 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
463._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Miller, Loeb 1913, De Officiis I.61-91). Partial match: Cicero speaks of danger in war and public affairs, not of risking one's capital in business, but the principle of weighing hazard against expected advantage is the same.

483.quote_or_event: “Further, there can be no doubt that a work is spoilt when not done at the right time? … the husbandman will not make his own plough or mattock, or other implements of agriculture, if they are to be good for anything.”
483.explanation: Founding the first city in speech, Socrates argues that work is ruined if its moment is let slip, and that each worker needs good implements made by others, so smiths and carpenters must join the city.
483.tie_back: The right time and the right implements, the Kural's kaalam and karuvi, appear together as the two conditions of successful work.
483.source: Plato, Republic, Book II, 370b–c (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
483._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Republic Book II); the ellipsis omits intervening dialogue. Plato pairs timing and tools in the context of the division of labour; he does not make the Kural's claim that with both nothing is impossible.

484.quote_or_event: “Without that opportunity their powers of mind would have been extinguished, and without those powers the opportunity would have come in vain.”
484.explanation: Machiavelli says Moses, Cyrus, Romulus and Theseus owed nothing to fortune but opportunity: Cyrus, for example, had to find the Persians discontented with the Medes and the Medes softened by long peace before he could found his empire.
484.tie_back: As in the Kural, the winning of great kingdoms depends on acting when time and circumstance are right.
484.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. VI (tr. W. K. Marriott)
484._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Marriott's translation on Project Gutenberg (eBook #1232). Strong on time and opportunity as the condition of conquest; the Kural's 'place' is matched only loosely by Machiavelli's circumstances, not by terrain.

502.quote_or_event: “In any office of trust or stewardship, on the other hand, the opposite rule should be observed; for more virtue than ordinary is required in the holder of such an office, but the necessary knowledge is of a sort which all men possess.”
502.explanation: Aristotle names loyalty to the constitution, administrative capacity and virtue as the qualifications for high office, and says that posts of trust call above all for exceptional virtue.
502.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle makes character, not skill alone, the test of whom a ruler should trust.
502.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book V, ch. 9 (1309a–b) (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
502._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Politics Book V, Part IX). Partial match: Aristotle shares the emphasis on virtue in those entrusted with office, but has nothing on good family or on the sense of shame (naan) that the Kural stresses.

542.quote_or_event: “He is the bond which fastens the commonwealth together, he is the breath of life to all those thousands, who by themselves would become merely an encumbrance and a source of plunder if that directing mind were withdrawn”
542.explanation: Writing to Nero, Seneca compares the ruler to the mind that directs the body and says the great multitude lives by him and would fall into ruin without him.
542.tie_back: Like the Kural's image of all life looking to the rain, Seneca makes the ruler the very breath by which the people live.
542.source: Seneca, Of Clemency (De Clementia), Book I, ch. 4 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
542._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Clemency, Book I). Strong match on the people's total dependence on the ruler; Seneca's image is breath and mind rather than rain, and his stress is on the ruler's direction rather than specifically on just rule.

544.quote_or_event: “That man's greatness alone rests upon a secure foundation, whom all men know to be as much on their side as he is above them … at whose approach they do not fly in terror, as though some evil and dangerous animal had sprung out from its den, but flock to him as they would to the bright and health-giving sunshine.”
544.explanation: Seneca adds that the subjects of such a ruler guard his sleep, surround and defend him, and offer their own bodies to protect him.
544.tie_back: The ruler who stands on his people's side is held fast by them, as the Kural's world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people.
544.source: Seneca, Of Clemency (De Clementia), Book I, ch. 3 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
544._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Clemency, Book I); the ellipsis omits a clause about the ruler's daily care for his subjects' safety. Close match on the reciprocity of a caring ruler and devoted subjects.

545.quote_or_event: “But those officers whose land he sees lying idle and with but few inhabitants, owing either to the harshness of their government, their insolence, or their neglect, he punishes, and making them to cease from their office he appoints other rulers in their place.”
545.explanation: Socrates tells Critobulus that the Persian king rewards governors whose districts are thickly peopled and richly cultivated, and removes those whose land lies waste through harsh or careless rule.
545.tie_back: Like the Kural, Xenophon ties the fruitfulness of a land to the quality of its government, though through administration rather than seasonal rain.
545.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus (The Economist), ch. IV, 8 (tr. H. G. Dakyns)
545._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Dakyns' translation on Project Gutenberg (eBook #1173). Partial match: the link between good government and abundant harvests is explicit, but it works through policy and oversight, with no cosmic or seasonal element.

546.quote_or_event: “But, of all motives, none is better adapted to secure influence and hold it fast than love; nothing is more foreign to that end than fear.”
546.explanation: Cicero argues that no amount of armed power can withstand the hatred of the many, as the fate of tyrants shows, while the affection won by just rule keeps power safe for ever.
546.tie_back: Lasting victory comes from just rule that wins the people, not from force, which is the Kural's sceptre set above the spear.
546.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §23 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
546._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Miller, Loeb 1913, De Officiis II.1-43). Strong match on force versus the goodwill that just rule earns; Cicero speaks of holding power rather than winning wars.

548.quote_or_event: “An old woman once assailed Demetrius as he was passing by, and demanded many times that he give her a hearing. ‘I have no time,’ said Demetrius. ‘Then don't be king,’ screamed the old woman.”
548.explanation: Plutarch says Demetrius was hard to approach, kept embassies waiting for years and threw his subjects' petitions into a river, so that the Macedonians felt insulted rather than ruled; soon afterwards his army deserted him and he lost Macedonia.
548.tie_back: The king who cannot be reached and will not hear complaints undoes his own kingdom, exactly as the Kural warns.
548.source: Plutarch, Life of Demetrius, ch. 42 (tr. Bernadotte Perrin)
548._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Perrin, Loeb 1920); inner double quotation marks rendered as single quotes. Near one-to-one: inaccessibility and neglect of justice, followed by the loss of the kingdom through the subjects' desertion (ch. 44), though rival kings also attacked him.

559.quote_or_event: “… they appeared glorious and blessed at the very time when they were full of avarice and unrighteous power. Zeus, the god of gods, who rules according to law, and is able to see into such things, perceiving that an honourable race was in a woeful plight, and wanting to inflict punishment on them …”
559.explanation: Critias tells how the kings of Atlantis, once just and obedient to law, grew greedy and unjust, so that Zeus resolved to punish them; the dialogue opens by recalling that the island was later sunk by an earthquake.
559.tie_back: Plato links the injustice of rulers to a cosmic punishment of their whole land, a distant parallel to the Kural's failed seasons and rain.
559._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett). Next-best match: the dialogue breaks off before the punishment, and there is no mention of rain or seasons; the shared idea is only that unjust rule brings divine ruin on the land.

572.quote_or_event: “… as men, too, are born for the sake of men, that they may be able mutually to help one another; in this direction we ought to follow Nature as our guide, to contribute to the general good by an interchange of acts of kindness, by giving and receiving …”
572.explanation: Cicero says human society is held together by mutual kindness, and a few sections later calls those who keep to their own affairs and give society nothing traitors to social life.
572.tie_back: As in the Kural, the world's business runs on kindly regard, and those who withhold it contribute nothing to the life they share.
572.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §§22, 29 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
572._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Miller, Loeb 1913, De Officiis I.20-41); the quoted words are from §22, and §29 is paraphrased in the explanation. Strong match on kindness as the bond of society; Cicero's 'traitors to social life' is close to, but less stark than, the Kural's 'burden on the earth'.

577.quote_or_event: “He is a runaway, who flies from social reason; he is blind, who shuts the eyes of the understanding; … he is a piece rent asunder from the state, who tears his own soul from that of reasonable animals, which is one.”
577.explanation: Marcus lists the ways a person fails his own nature: whoever cuts himself off from the shared reason and fellowship of rational beings is a fugitive, blind, and torn from the whole.
577.tie_back: Like the Kural, Marcus calls the one who withdraws from fellow-feeling blind, though his blindness is of the understanding rather than a lack of kindly regard.
577.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV, §29 (tr. George Long)
577._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long); the ellipsis omits one clause. Next-best match: the shared image is blindness in one who cuts himself off from others, but Marcus's emphasis is on social reason, not on graciousness or compassion.

595.quote_or_event: “… it makes a material for itself out of that which opposes it, as fire lays hold of what falls into it, by which a small light would have been extinguished: but when the fire is strong, it soon appropriates to itself the matter which is heaped on it, and consumes it, and rises higher by means of this very material.”
595.explanation: Marcus says the ruling part of the mind, when it follows nature, turns every obstacle into fuel, as a strong fire feeds on what would smother a weak one.
595.tie_back: Both use an image from nature in which the strength of the inner force decides how high one rises: the stalk with the water, the flame with its own strength.
595.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV, §1 (tr. George Long)
595._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long). Partial match: Marcus's point is the mind's power to use adversity, whereas the Kural says one's height matches one's energy of mind; the overlap is the image of inner strength determining how high one rises.

599.quote_or_event: Rallying the Greek officers after their generals had been seized by the Persians, Xenophon tells them that it is neither numbers nor strength that wins victories in war: whichever side advances with the stronger spirit, its enemies as a rule will not stand against it.
599.explanation: Xenophon urges the officers to restore the courage of their troops, since morale, not size, decides battles.
599.tie_back: Like the tiger routing the huge, tusked elephant, the side with the stronger spirit prevails over sheer bulk.
599.source: Xenophon, Anabasis, Book III, ch. 1, §42 (tr. H. G. Dakyns)
599._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the Book III text could not be loaded this session to verify wording, so no quotation is given. Strong match on spirit outweighing size and strength; Xenophon speaks of armies, not single animals.

university.483: The couplet is a rhetorical question: aruvinai enpa ulavo, ‘are there things one could call hard deeds?’ The condition has two parts, karuviyaan (by means of instruments) and kaalam arindhu (knowing the time). Parimelazhagar takes karuvi to mean the resources of the state, such as army and treasury, together with the right methods. Neither timing without means nor means without timing is enough. The printed spelling ‘yenpa’ reflects sandhi with the preceding vowel; the word is enpa.
university.1012: Oon (ஊண், 'food'), udai (உடை, 'clothing') and echcham (எச்சம், 'the remainder', i.e. the other bodily needs) are veralla (வேறல்ல, 'not different') for all uyir (உயிர், 'living beings'). By contrast naanudaimai (நாணுடைமை, 'the possession of shame') is maandhar sirappu (மாந்தர் சிறப்பு, 'the distinction of humans'). Kesikan and Varadarasanar take the first line to cover all beings and sets of people. Pappaiah narrows the contrast: food and clothing are common to all people, while shame distinguishes the good. Kalaignar explains naanudaimai as avoiding what others condemn. The kural thus makes shame the defining mark of the human, an idea that echoes widely in Indian (Hitopadesha) and Greek (Protagoras) ethics. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.
